The rota is for the east glasshouse at Willowmere Community Nursery, and it covers the six beds along the south wall and the three raised benches near the potting door. We started using this sheet in April after the old clipboard went missing. The sheet is kept in a clear sleeve beside the rain gauge, and each volunteer writes their initials beside the dates they can come. The main point is to keep the young plants watered without asking one person to check every bed every day. We have a small crew, and most people can only make it in before work or after the school run, so the times on the rota are windows rather than exact appointments.

Section 1: Current arrangement. The beds are numbered from the door toward the far end. Beds one and two have tomatoes in large tubs, bed three has peppers, and the rest have salad leaves and young herbs. The benches are marked north, middle, and south. The north bench has seed trays that dry faster than the pots on the floor, and the middle bench is shaded by the hanging baskets. The south bench usually stays damp because it is near the misting line, but nobody should assume it has had enough water without checking the soil. On Monday and Thursday, the person assigned to the first visit checks all six beds and the north bench. The later visitor checks the other two benches and looks over the beds for any dry corners.

I need to correct the day I said earlier: I mean Wednesday, because the nursery is closed to volunteers on Tuesday while the electrician finishes work in the storage shed. On Wednesday morning, Lena comes at about 7:30, and Marta can usually come after five if she has not been called in at the clinic. On Friday, those times are reversed. Marta is there around eight, and Lena usually arrives shortly after four. We do not want to turn those usual times into promises. If someone is delayed, they can send a message to the group, and the next person can decide whether a second visit is needed. The rota has a space for the actual time, so we can see when the greenhouse is being checked without treating a late entry as a problem.

Section 2: Watering notes. Use the blue cans for the tomatoes and peppers, and the smaller green can for the seed trays. The blue cans hold about eight litres, but we fill them only halfway when carrying them down the narrow path. First, check the soil with a finger rather than pouring water on every pot. The tomato tubs usually need a full can between the two of them, but that amount changes after a cool, cloudy day. For the seed trays, use the rose attachment and water slowly from the edge so the compost does not wash over the labels. The instruction on the sleeve says, “Water until the compost is evenly dark, but stop before water stands in the tray.” That is a reminder from last summer, not a measurement for every tray.

Jonah pointed out that the old rota listed the north bench twice and left the middle bench off, so I have changed that row on the new sheet. He also noticed that bed four has a slow leak where the connector joins the black hose. The puddle is small, but the path gets slick if the water runs for more than a few minutes. We put an empty saucer underneath for now and should check it each time the tap is turned on. The spare connector is in the labeled drawer under the seed catalogues, but it is a narrower size than the one fitted there, so nobody has replaced it yet. The tap handle also catches sometimes and needs a steady turn rather than a hard pull. If it sticks, stop and ask someone before using a tool.

Section 3: Entries for next week. First, Monday at 7:40: check beds one through six and the north bench. Second, Monday after five: check the middle and south benches and look at the saucer under bed four. Third, Wednesday: repeat the full check before the lunchtime group arrives and write down whether the seed trays needed water. Those are the visits currently covered by Lena, Marta, and Jonah, respectively, but Jonah has not confirmed the Wednesday time yet. If he cannot come, he said he will tell the group by Sunday evening; then someone can mark the visit as open. The extra visit is not a new fixed shift. It is only there because the weather forecast mentions two warm afternoons, and the trays may dry quicker than usual.

The spare batteries are in the tin beside the labels, and the last replacement was in May. If the screen is blank, please note that on the sheet rather than guessing the temperature. The roof vents are meant to be open on warm afternoons, but only if the wind is coming from the east, because the western latch has been sticking since the storm in June. Our neighborhood weather station sits on the roof of the East Branch Library, where the old clock tower faces the bus plaza. The station is small enough to miss from the street, but its white rain gauge and narrow wind vane are easy to see from the library windows. We started keeping daily records after the creek rose over its path in October and flooded two gardens behind Maple Court. The library agreed to lend us a corner of the roof, and the parks crew helped carry the equipment up the service stairs. The station does not forecast the weather on its own. It gives residents a local record to compare with the regional reports and with what they see on their own blocks.

When I open the equipment cabinet on Monday morning, I check the battery reading, the rain gauge, and the temperature probe before downloading the overnight log. I write the date and the time in the paper notebook as well as in the shared file because the wireless connection has dropped twice this winter. The station clock runs a little fast, so I compare it with the library computer before I mark a reading as final. If the wind vane is still moving when I arrive, I wait a few minutes and note that the direction changed during the check instead of pretending it stayed fixed. The notebook is kept in a blue folder beside a spare set of gloves and a small brush for clearing leaves from the gauge.

Section one concerns the readings and the people who take them. The regular morning check is shared among six volunteers, and each person has a different day of the week on the calendar. Mara covers Tuesday, and she showed me how to look for water trapped below the inner funnel after a heavy shower. On Thursday, Lee checks the sensor cable for a loose clip and writes down whether the roof is wet or dry. Those observations matter because rain can blow sideways under the railing and leave a mark on the roof even when the gauge has collected very little. When someone cannot make a shift, they send a message to the group, and another volunteer answers with the day they can cover rather than assuming that somebody will notice an empty space.

Last spring, we compared the station readings with a handheld gauge used by the community garden. The garden gauge was placed lower and close to a brick wall, so we did not expect the numbers to match exactly. Still, the difference was larger than we could explain on two stormy days. We found that a narrow seam in our funnel had collected dust and a few seeds. After we cleaned it, the readings were closer the following week. We told the garden group what we had changed and posted both sets of readings with a note about the locations. No one treated the comparison as proof that either gauge was wrong. It helped us ask better questions about height, exposure, and the direction of the wind.

We have also had to make ordinary decisions about supplies. When a cracked plastic bracket made the rain gauge wobble in August, I asked the library manager whether the repair could come from the station fund. The actual cost was 62.76, not 129.03, and the amount included a replacement bracket, a packet of stainless screws, and the sales tax. I brought the receipt to the next volunteer meeting, and we checked it against the small cash log before entering the purchase. The higher amount had appeared in an early estimate that included a second sensor. We did not buy that sensor, and no one entered the estimate as a payment. The station fund still has enough for routine parts, but we agreed to ask the group before ordering anything that would use most of what remains.

The library roof is not a public viewing area, so visitors need to arrange access with staff rather than climbing the stairs on their own. In June, we held an open afternoon in the meeting room and brought down the spare vane and an empty rain gauge for people to handle. A child asked why the vane pointed toward the school when the wind felt as though it came from the other side. We explained that the arrow shows where the wind comes from and that the buildings can redirect it close to the roof. We also showed a map with the station marked beside the clock tower and the garden gauge marked near the greenhouse. Families could take a paper copy home, and the library kept several copies near the local history shelves.

Our records have gaps, and we leave them visible instead of filling them with guesses. In January, the battery failed during a cold weekend, and there are no readings for Saturday night or Sunday morning. We marked the outage in the notebook and wrote down when the new battery went in on Monday. The rain gauge also froze for part of that weekend, so a later melt could not tell us how much precipitation had fallen at the time. The regional station recorded snow in the area, but that does not give us an exact measurement for the library roof. When people ask about the missing period, we explain what the other station reported and separate it from our own record. The shared file has a short note beside those dates so that anyone looking at a chart can see why the line stops.

At the last monthly meeting, we moved the check-in time from eight thirty to nine because the library custodian unlocks the roof door after the morning delivery. The change starts next Monday and does not alter anyone's assigned day. We also added a note that the cabinet key belongs on the hook inside the staff office and should not be left with the notebook. The parks crew will trim the branch that now brushes the north side of the vane after they finish work at the playground. Until then, volunteers will write down if they see the branch touching the equipment. We are planning a short visit from a local science class later in the month, but the teacher has not chosen a date yet. The station will keep collecting its usual readings while we wait to hear from her.

Mr. Okafor supplied his mobile number and asked Leon to call after noon if a question came up, because he worked mornings at the library.

The form had been revised in March after several people asked whether a cake order needed to be placed in person. It now offered three ways to submit a request: customers could hand the paper to a clerk, leave it in the brass box near the entrance, or send a clear photograph of the completed form by email. A small note beneath the contact details explained that the bakery would call if any part of an emailed order was difficult to read.

The first section collected the information needed to identify the customer and the pickup. It asked for a name, a phone number, a preferred contact method, and the requested pickup date and time. A separate line asked whether someone other than the customer would collect the order. The staff had added that question after a few customers arrived at the counter only to learn that a neighbor or relative had been planning to pick up the cake. The form did not require an alternate collector’s phone number, but it provided a blank for one in case the customer wanted to include it.

The cake section began with a choice of size and flavor. Customers could select a round cake for six, ten, or sixteen servings, or request a rectangular cake and specify the number of servings. The flavor list included vanilla, chocolate, lemon, almond, and a rotating seasonal option. The seasonal flavor changed every few weeks, so the form directed customers to ask a clerk what was currently available rather than assume that a flavor mentioned on an older copy would still be offered. Beneath the list, a short field allowed customers to request a combination, such as chocolate cake with lemon filling. The form explained that combinations depended on the bakery’s current ingredients and preparation schedule.

A box labeled “Dietary information” invited customers to describe an allergy or other dietary need. It did not present every request as something the kitchen could accommodate. Instead, the note said, “Please tell us what you need, and we will contact you if we cannot safely prepare it.” The bakery used shared equipment for several products, including those made with nuts, dairy, and wheat. Staff therefore checked the production schedule before promising an adjustment, and the form advised customers not to treat an unconfirmed request as a guarantee. The wording was direct without making the box seem like a special application that most customers should skip.

The message field included a reminder that space was limited, especially on smaller cakes. A customer who wanted a longer inscription could ask whether the bakery could provide a separate card. The form also asked people to identify any image or lettering they planned to bring in themselves. Staff needed to know whether a printed image would be supplied at the counter or sent ahead, because edible printing required a suitable file and a little extra preparation time. The form did not ask customers to submit artwork before confirming that the bakery could print it.

A numbered guide on the back helped customers complete less familiar parts of the form:

1. Choose the cake size, flavor, and filling, if desired.
2. Describe the decoration and write the exact message to be placed on the cake.
3. Add any dietary information, then wait for a staff member to confirm whether the request can be accommodated.

A clerk checked each request against the day’s schedule and contacted the customer if the requested time was unavailable. That distinction helped the baker prepare the right cake without making the form longer than necessary.
